introduction: The Physical Education School-Based Assessment has both a practical and a written element: you are assessed on your performance in selected practical activities and on a personal exercise programme or investigation that you plan, carry out over several weeks, record and evaluate. Marks are given for your planning and risk management, your fitness testing and records, the suitability of the programme, your performance improvement and your evaluation. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the number of activities and the exact format required.

tasks.title: Test battery
tasks.explanation: Record your baseline scores on at least four fitness components using standard tests, describing the protocol, the equipment and the conditions for each.

tasks.title: Strengths and weaknesses
tasks.explanation: Compare your results with norms for your age and sex and with the demands of your sport or activity, and identify your two weakest components.

tasks.title: Personal exercise programme
tasks.explanation: Write a six- to eight-week programme showing frequency, intensity, time, type and progression for each session, and explain how it applies the principles of training.

tasks.title: Safety plan
tasks.explanation: Identify the risks of the activities, state the control measures, and describe warm-up, cool-down, hydration and emergency procedures.

tasks.title: Activity performance
tasks.explanation: Perform in the selected practical activities, demonstrating correct technique, tactical awareness, rules, fair play and cooperation with others.

tasks.title: Retest and review
tasks.explanation: Retest the components, present before-and-after results in a table or graph, evaluate what improved and what did not, explain why, and recommend changes to the programme.

sampleTitle: An eight-week programme to improve a 400 m runner's speed endurance and core strength

sample.body: Frequency: four sessions a week (two track, one circuit, one games session). Intensity: interval work at 80-90 per cent of maximum heart rate in weeks 3 to 6, reduced in week 8 for competition. Time: 60-75 minutes including warm-up and cool-down. Type: 200 m and 300 m repetitions with 2-3 minute recoveries to develop speed endurance (anaerobic system), circuit training of 8 stations for core and leg strength, and continuous jogging for aerobic base. Progression: repetitions rise from 4 x 200 m in week 1 to 6 x 300 m in week 5, while recovery time falls from 3 to 2 minutes. Specificity: interval distances and recovery ratios match the demands of the 400 m event, and the circuit focuses on the trunk and hip muscles used in sprinting.
sample.tips: Every principle of training named in the plan earns marks, and the reason must link to the event.

sample.body: The 30 m sprint time fell from 4.5 s to 4.2 s and the Illinois agility run from 17.1 s to 16.2 s, and the 400 m time improved by 3.4 s. The sit and reach score did not change because the programme contained no flexibility work beyond the cool-down stretch - a clear planning error. Two sessions were missed in week 4 because of rain and a school event, which showed how easy reversibility is. Improvement: add two dedicated flexibility sessions and a contingency plan for wet weather, since the runs had to be completed in the final week to complete the volume.
sample.tips: Use the before-and-after numbers, name the specific weaknesses in your own plan and say what you will change.

marking: Marks reward a properly conducted baseline test, accurate interpretation of results against norms, a programme that applies the principles of training and matches the activity, thorough safety planning, good practical technique and fair play, and a candid, evidence-based evaluation with recommendations.
checklist: At least four fitness components tested with protocols described
Results recorded with dates and conditions
Programme states FITT for every session
Practical performance assessed in the chosen activity

categories.comment: Six components are tested rather than four, and every score is recorded with its protocol, equipment, surface, temperature and time of day, so the retest can be compared fairly.

Baseline scores are converted to a score relative to the age norm so that a sprint time and a plank hold can be compared on one scale, and the two weakest components are named and used to decide the programme.

The eight-week plan states frequency, intensity, time and type for every key session, raises one variable at a time, and explains specificity, overload, progression, reversibility and recovery against the actual sessions.
Six hazards are listed with practical control measures, and warm-up, cool-down, hydration, heat and the emergency procedure are all written down before the programme starts.

Technique, tactics, rules, fair play and cooperation are each evidenced: pacing and posture in the 400 m, an even race plan, honest times including two self-corrected splits, and pacing a teammate returning from illness.

The retest repeats the battery in the same conditions, reports the two targeted gains, explains the component that did not change as specificity rather than failure, and names the weaker baseline timing as the portfolio's own limitation.

pages.heading: Cover page and contents of this Physical Education SBA
pages.body: This portfolio is a complete worked example of the Physical Education School-Based Assessment: a baseline test battery, an analysis against age norms, an eight-week personal exercise programme written on the guide's own sampleTitle (improving a 400 m runner's speed endurance and core strength), a safety and risk plan, the practical performance record, and a candid evaluation against a retest. The candidate, the school, the coach, the training group and every score in it are invented for CSEC Compass, and all of the data is internally consistent: every percentage change, relative score and rating in this portfolio is calculated from the scores in the tables.

pages.heading: Method: how the tests were planned, run and recorded
pages.body:
Method: how the tests were planned, run and recorded. Nothing in this portfolio was improvised. The eight-week programme was written only after a baseline week, and the baseline week was planned so that the scores would mean something when the programme was over. Six components were tested rather than the four required in our guide, because the plan needed to separate speed endurance and core strength from general aerobic fitness: if those two were weak and general endurance was strong, that would tell the programme to be specific rather than simply harder.

Every test was carried out on the same day of the week, at the same time, after the same 15-minute warm-up, and each was recorded with the date, the temperature and the surface. Timed runs were hand-timed by the coach with a second timer as a check, and the sit-up and plank tests used the same mat and the same holder on both test days. The retest in week 9 repeated the battery in the same order and the same conditions, so that any change in the results comes from the training rather than from the day. The full battery, with protocol and equipment, is in the next part, and every score was written into the log sheet on the day it was taken, not from memory afterwards.
bullets: Same day of the week, same time, same 15-minute warm-up, conditions recorded with every score
Six components tested so speed endurance could be separated from general aerobic fitness
Retest repeats the battery in the same order so the comparison means something

pages.heading: Fitness Testing and Baseline: the six tests used
pages.body:
Fitness Testing and Baseline: the six tests and why each was chosen. The battery covers speed, speed endurance, aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, core strength and flexibility. Only the first five are trained by the programme; flexibility was tested because it is part of a complete picture and because it gives the evaluation something honest to say about an untrained component.

The protocols matter as much as the scores. The 300 m time trial was run as a single effort with a long recovery, because a second effort would be affected by the first. The 12-minute run was measured in laps and part-laps on a 400 m circuit so that distance could be read off the sheet. The plank hold was stopped at the first loss of hip alignment rather than at the point of collapse, which is why the number is smaller than it might have been: the test measures control, not stubbornness. Conditions are recorded with each score so that the retest can be compared fairly.

pages.heading: Results: baseline scores compared with the age norms
pages.body: The baseline table scores every component against the age norm on one scale, so a sprint time and a plank hold can be compared directly. Above 100 per cent means better than the norm. On this evidence the runner has a trained aerobic base and a top-end speed that is on the norm, and the two components that decide a 400 m race, speed endurance and core strength, are the ones below it.

table.caption: Baseline scores compared with norms for a 16-year-old in the same event group

pages.heading: Analysis of Results: strengths, weaknesses and what the programme must target
pages.body:
Analysis of Results: strengths, weaknesses and what the programme must target. Baseline scores were converted to a score relative to the age norm, so that a fast time and a long hold could be compared on one scale. Read that way, the picture is clear. Aerobic endurance and muscular endurance were both above the norm at 107.8 per cent and 108.6 per cent, and speed was on the norm at 99.6 per cent, so the runner already has a base and can hold a rhythm. The two weakest components were core strength at 79.5 per cent, well below the norm, and speed endurance at 93.1 per cent, below it. Flexibility sat exactly on the norm at 100 per cent.

That ordering decides the programme. A 400 m runner who cannot hold trunk posture in the third 100 m loses form exactly where the race is decided, and a 300 m time trial slower than the norm relative to a 30 m sprint that is on the norm means the drop-off over distance, not top-end speed, is the limit. The programme therefore spends its quality sessions on speed endurance and its supplementary work on core strength, while general aerobic work is maintained with easy running only. Flexibility is not targeted, and the evaluation says so rather than pretending every component improved.
bullets: Strengths: aerobic endurance (107.8% of norm) and muscular endurance (108.6%); speed on the norm (99.6%)
Weakest two: core strength (79.5% of norm) and speed endurance (93.1%) - the two the programme targets
Flexibility sits on the norm (100.0%) and is not trained by this programme

pages.heading: Programme Planning: the eight-week programme
pages.body:
Programme Planning: the eight-week programme and the principles it applies. The programme runs three quality sessions and two easy sessions a week, with one full rest day. Every key session states frequency, intensity, time and type, and progression is written into the plan rather than decided on the day, so that overload rises in one variable at a time.

Five principles carry the plan. Specificity: the work moves from 4 x 200 m to 3 x 300 m to 2 x 350 m, so the final weeks rehearse the race distance and the recovery it demands. Overload: the number of repetitions, the duration of the core holds and the intensity all rise week by week, never two of them in the same week. Progression: week 7 cuts volume by a third so the retest is run fresh, which is progression by design rather than by accident. Reversibility: the easy runs on the two non-quality days keep the aerobic base that was already above the norm. Recovery: quality sessions are separated by at least one easy day, because speed endurance is built in the recovery between sessions, not only in the sessions themselves.

The core work follows the same logic at a smaller scale. Weeks 3 to 5 raise time under tension from 12 to 18 minutes with the same exercises, and only the final weeks add difficulty. This is the component the baseline showed to be weakest, so it also gets the highest frequency, four short sessions rather than one long one.

pages.heading: Safety and Risk Management: the risk assessment and safety plan
pages.body:
Safety and Risk Management: the risks of this programme and how each was controlled. The programme was approved by the school's athletics teacher, and the teacher or another member of staff was present at every session. Before the plan started, the candidate completed the school's medical declaration and confirmed that there was no known heart or joint condition that fast running would aggravate.

The main hazards are the ones that come with maximal speed and repeated core work: a hamstring strain from sprinting on cold muscles, overuse soreness from four core sessions a week, heat illness in afternoon sessions, dehydration and cramp, and an ankle injury on the grass circuit. Each is controlled in the table below, and the controls are practical rather than aspirational: the 15-minute warm-up with strides cannot be skipped on a fast day, water is at every session, sessions move later in the afternoon or are cancelled above 32 C, and the circuit is walked for holes before each session. The emergency procedure is also written down before it is needed: stop the session, apply RICE, tell the teacher, contact the parent, and record what happened in the log sheet the same day. A suspected muscle tear is not run through, and a session lost to injury is a session to be rebuilt, not made up in the same week.

pages.heading: Practical Performance: the activities assessed
pages.body:
Practical Performance: the activities assessed and how they were performed. Four things are assessed here: technique, tactical awareness, knowledge and application of the rules, and cooperation and fair play. The main activity is the 400 m, supported by the relay, the speed endurance sessions and the core circuit, because those are the activities the programme was written for.

Technique was judged on pacing and posture: opening the first 200 m under control rather than flat out, holding trunk position through the third 100 m, and finishing without the shoulders dropping. Tactics were judged on the race plan itself, which changed during the programme from a fast start that faded to an even split. Rules and fair play were assessed in competition and in training: times were recorded honestly, including the two split times that were entered wrongly and then corrected on the log sheet, and no session was run at an intensity the plan did not ask for. Cooperation was assessed across the training group: timing a teammate's reps without being asked, and pacing a teammate returning from illness in week 5.

pages.heading: Results: the retest compared with the baseline
pages.body: The retest was taken in week 9, in the same order and the same conditions as the baseline. Five components improved and one moved by 1 cm, which is inside the measurement error of the test. The 400 m race time is included as the outcome that matters: the fitness change only counts if it reaches the event.

table.caption: Retest (week 9) compared with the baseline (week 0). A change no larger than the test's own measurement error is reported as no change, so the flexibility row reads 'within measurement error' rather than as a gain.

pages.heading: Discussion: what improved, what did not, and why
pages.body:
Discussion: what improved, what did not, and why. Five of the six components improved, and the two the programme targeted improved the most, which is the evidence that the plan worked rather than that the candidate simply got fitter. Core strength rose from 62 s to 88 s, a gain of 41.9 per cent, on a plank test that measures control and was stopped at the first loss of alignment both times, so the number is comparable. Speed endurance improved from 47.8 s to 45.9 s over 300 m, 4.0 per cent faster, and muscular endurance rose 15.8 per cent. The transfer to the event is the point of the whole programme: the 400 m time came down from 61.4 s to 58.9 s, and the improvement came from holding form in the third 100 m rather than from a faster start.

The two components that did not change much are equally informative. Aerobic endurance improved least of the trained components, up 5.2 per cent, which is exactly what specificity predicts: the plan maintained aerobic work with easy running and spent its overload on speed endurance, so the untrained-for-purpose component improved only through general conditioning. Flexibility moved by 1 cm, from 24 to 25 cm, which is inside the measurement error of a sit-and-reach test and is honestly reported as no change, because the programme did not train it. Neither result is a failure of the plan; both are the plan behaving as written, and both are the reason the evaluation can trust the two large gains.

A third lesson is about measurement. The baseline 300 m trial was hand-timed with a single timer, and the coach noted afterwards that a second timer should have been used from week 0, not from week 4. The retest used two timers and both agreed to 0.1 s, so the comparison holds, but the weakest link in this portfolio is timing accuracy and it is named here rather than hidden.
bullets: Biggest gains in the two targeted components: core strength 41.9%, speed endurance 4.0% faster
Aerobic endurance improved least of the trained components (5.2%) - specificity working as written
Flexibility changed by 1 cm, inside measurement error, and is reported as no change
Weakest link named honestly: hand-timing at the baseline before the two-timer check was introduced

pages.heading: Conclusion: evaluation and recommendations for the next programme
pages.body:
Conclusion: what the programme achieved and what should change next. The eight-week programme met its purpose. Speed endurance improved by 4.0 per cent over 300 m and core strength by 41.9 per cent, the two components the baseline identified as weakest, and the 400 m race time fell by 2.5 s to 58.9 s with the improvement in the third 100 m rather than in the start. Aerobic endurance and muscular endurance, already above the norm, were maintained, and flexibility was left essentially unchanged.

Four changes would improve the next programme. First, two timers from the baseline onwards, so that timing accuracy is never the weakest part of the evidence. Second, a flexibility session twice a week, since eight weeks of ignoring it produced no change at all and a sprinter's hamstrings pay for that later. Third, the core progression in weeks 5 to 7 can start a week earlier: 88 s at the retest was still short of the 100 s target, which suggests the base phase was conservative rather than that the ceiling was reached. Fourth, the aerobic easy runs should be given a weekly distance target, because the 12-minute run improved least of the trained components and the easy sessions were the least planned part of the week.

The programme is repeatable. The battery, the conditions and the log sheet are all recorded, so the next eight weeks can begin from 88 s and 45.9 s rather than from an estimate, and the comparison will be honest for the same reason this one was: same tests, same order, same conditions, and every number written down on the day.
bullets: Programme purpose met: 400 m from 61.4 s to 58.9 s, with the gain in the third 100 m
Targets hit: speed endurance 45.9 s over 300 m, core strength 88 s plank
First recommendation: two timers from the baseline, so timing is never the weakest evidence
Next block starts from 88 s and 45.9 s, on the same battery and the same conditions

pages.heading: Sources and honesty note for this worked example
pages.body: Every score, date, condition, name and place in this portfolio is invented for CSEC Compass. The candidate, the centre, the coach, the training group and the training times are all made up, and the test protocols are written out in full so that a reader can see they are the ordinary school tests rather than laboratory procedures. Nothing here is taken from another candidate's portfolio, from a published training plan, or from any examination material. The purpose of the sample is to show the shape of a strong Physical Education SBA: a baseline taken under recorded conditions, results compared with norms and read honestly, a programme that targets what the baseline found weak and states FITT for every key session, a safety plan written before it is needed, practical performance assessed against the criteria, and an evaluation that reports the components which did not improve as clearly as the ones that did. Use it for the method, and take your own baseline before you plan anything.
bullets: All scores, names and conditions invented; nothing reproduced from another portfolio or published plan
All percentages, relative scores and ratings computed from the tables in this portfolio
Reusable method: baseline under recorded conditions, programme from the analysis, retest in the same conditions

examinerNotes: The programme is decided by the baseline rather than by preference: the two components scored lowest against the age norm are exactly the two the plan overloads, and every other component is maintained.
Frequency, intensity, time and type are stated for each key session in plain numbers, and progression is written into the plan, so the candidate is not inventing the next step on the day.

The evaluation is candid: it reports a 1 cm change in an untrained component as no change, explains the smallest gain as specificity, and names hand-timing at the baseline as the weakest part of the evidence.
Practical performance is evidenced with behaviour as well as scores: self-corrected split times, timing a teammate's reps unprompted, and pacing a returning teammate in week 5.
